findings.title: Negative-offset pagination crashes because Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative slice bounds (raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this path will always raise at runtime rather than 'enable efficient bidirectional pagination' as the comments claim ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false). Any admin/superuser request that hits `organization_auditlogs.py` with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor whose offset is negative will 500. There is no test exercising this branch, so the bug would ship undetected.

findings.title: Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets instead of erroring, affecting all cursor paginators
findings.body: `BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and now `OptimizedCursorPaginator` — i.e. most cursor-paginated endpoints in the codebase) used to do `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` directly. The change introduces `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which silently clamps negative offsets to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of letting the previous (implicit) error surface. This changes pagination semantics for every endpoint built on `BasePaginator`, not just the audit log endpoint this PR is nominally about, and ships with no new/updated tests demonstrating the previous vs. new behavior across those call sites.

findings.title: New admin-gated 'optimized pagination' code path has no test coverage and is unrelated to stated PR scope
findings.body: A new branch is added that switches to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which enables the broken negative-offset code path) based on a client-supplied query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. This is a brand-new, security-sensitive conditional pagination feature introduced in a PR whose description and other changes are about the spans buffer. No tests were added for this branch, for the permission gating, or for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` itself, so none of this new logic (including the crash described separately) is verified before merge.

findings.title: Redirect-chain loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the explanatory warning comment
findings.body: The loop that follows redirect pointers (`for i = 0, 1000 do ... end`) was previously bounded at 10000 with a comment explaining that 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' The bound was cut to 1000 and the comment was deleted entirely. This makes it 10x more likely that deep redirect/segment trees fail to be joined correctly, and removes the only documentation warning future maintainers about this trade-off, with no corresponding test for deep trees near/above the new limit.

findings.title: max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code; segment size cap is a hardcoded magic number in Lua, decoupled from configuration
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the Python-side enforcement of this limit in `_load_segment_data` was removed entirely in this PR. The new eviction cap is hardcoded as the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', ...)`), completely independent of `self.max_segment_spans`. Callers who construct `SpansBuffer` with a custom `max_segment_spans` value will silently get no effect from that setting, which is a misleading public API and an operational trap for anyone trying to tune this value.

findings.title: Unconditional dict indexing on end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer on payloads missing the field
findings.body: `process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` via direct key access with no fallback, where `val` is the raw span payload deserialized from Kafka. If any ingested message lacks this field (e.g. during a rollout where Relay has not yet started populating it everywhere, replay of older backlog messages, or a malformed/older-schema payload), this raises `KeyError` and will crash/raise inside the batch-processing task, taking down the whole consumer batch rather than degrading gracefully. Given this is a critical ingestion pipeline, a schema-evolution-safe default (e.g. `.get('end_timestamp_precise', ...)`) or explicit validation should be used instead of hard failure.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new eviction behavior, including the risk of evicting the root span's payload
findings.body: The new eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`) removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. Since the root/segment span can legitimately have an earlier end timestamp than some of its children, it can be evicted by this logic while the separate `has_root_span` flag key still persists, causing `flush_segments` to report a segment as having a root span even though the root span's actual payload was dropped. No test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans or validates eviction/root-span-retention behavior, so this edge case is unverified.
